listeningScripts.title: Phone Plan Upgrade
listeningScripts.text: Customer: Hi, I'm interested in upgrading my phone plan. I currently have the basic plan with 2 GB of data. Support: Great! I can definitely help with that. What's your phone number? Customer: It's 416-555-0234. I'm constantly hitting my data limit, especially with streaming videos. Support: I understand. Let me pull up your account. You're right, your basic plan is 2 GB per month at $35. What data usage would work better for you? Customer: Probably something like 10 GB. How much would that be? Support: We have a 10 GB plan at $65 per month. You'd also get unlimited texting and more calling minutes. Would that interest you? Customer: What's the difference in calling minutes from my current plan? Support: Your current plan has 200 minutes; the 10 GB plan has unlimited calling. Plus, there's no contract change required if you cancel later. Customer: Actually, do you have an 8 GB plan? That might be better value. Support: Good question. We do have an 8 GB plan at $55 per month with the same unlimited calling and texting. Customer: Perfect, I'll take that. When does it take effect? Support: I'm activating it right now. Your bill will reflect the change next billing cycle, which is on July 8th. The monthly cost goes from $35 to $55. Customer: That works for me. Thanks.

listeningScripts.title: Music Concert Plans
listeningScripts.text: Alex: Are you going to the concert next Saturday? Casey: Which one? There are a few shows next weekend. Alex: The indie rock festival at the waterfront. Casey: Oh yeah, I've been thinking about it. How much are tickets? Alex: They're forty dollars each. Casey: That's not too bad. Who's performing? Alex: Five bands. The headliner is The Northern Stars. Casey: Oh, I love them. What time does it start? Alex: Six PM. It should wrap up around eleven. Casey: That's pretty late. Is there parking nearby? Alex: Yeah, there's a parking lot right by the venue. It's five dollars for the whole night. Casey: That's reasonable. Should we get food there or bring our own? Alex: They have food vendors there, but it's probably expensive. Casey: Let's grab something before we go then. Alex: Good idea. Want me to buy your ticket? Casey: Yeah, that would be great. Just send me the bill.

listeningScripts.title: Workplace Safety Training: Fire Procedures
listeningScripts.text: Good morning. This is your mandatory workplace fire safety training. Please listen carefully. In case of fire alarm, first, stay calm. Second, evacuate using the nearest exit. Do not use elevators under any circumstances. Stairs are located at both ends of each hallway. Third, move to the designated assembly point in the parking lot north of the building. Check in with your team leader. Fourth, do not re-enter the building until an authorized person announces it's safe. Fire drills occur quarterly on the first Friday of March, June, September, and December at 2 PM. During drills, the process is identical to a real emergency. Everyone must participate. If you cannot evacuate due to disability, proceed to a designated refuge area and use the emergency call button. These refuge areas are marked on building maps. Fire extinguishers are located every twenty-five meters along hallways and near kitchen areas. Only trained staff should operate extinguishers. If you're not trained, alert a supervisor. Report any fire hazards such as blocked exits or damaged equipment to maintenance immediately. Violations of fire safety procedures may result in disciplinary action. Contact Safety Services with any questions.

listeningScripts.title: Quebec Education Reform Approved
listeningScripts.text: The Quebec National Assembly has approved a major education reform bill with broad cross-party support. The legislation, Bill 247, focuses on modernizing curriculum standards and addressing teacher shortages. Under the new framework, high schools will introduce mandatory digital literacy courses starting next September. The reform also increases teacher salaries by 8 percent over four years to attract and retain educators. Currently, Quebec faces a shortage of approximately 3,500 teachers, particularly in mathematics, sciences, and French language instruction. The bill allocates 2.1 billion dollars for infrastructure improvements to school facilities. Education Minister Jean-François Roberge noted that 87 percent of school boards support the reforms. Parents will have increased choice in selecting specialized program options for their children. Pilot projects will begin in 15 schools across the province to test innovative teaching methods before full implementation in 2027.

listeningScripts.title: Small Business Loan Program Discussion
listeningScripts.text:
Bank Manager Chris: Our small business loan program has been quite successful this year. We've approved 285 loans totaling 42 million dollars to local entrepreneurs. However, we've noticed our default rate is slightly higher than industry average at about 4.2 percent. We're considering tightening our lending criteria to reduce risk.

Economic Development Officer Lisa: I would caution against tightening the criteria too much, Chris. These small loans are crucial for community development and job creation. Yes, a few borrowers struggle, but 95 percent of our loans are performing well. If we make the qualification requirements too strict, we'll only serve well-established businesses with existing collateral. That defeats the purpose of supporting new entrepreneurs who are taking real risks.

Business Owner Marcus: I completely agree with Lisa. When I started my restaurant five years ago, traditional banks wouldn't touch me because I didn't have significant assets or a ten-year track record. Your bank took a chance on me, and now my business employs 12 people. If your criteria were stricter, I wouldn't be here. I think what you should focus on is better support systems after lending, like mentorship programs and financial coaching.

Bank Manager Chris: Marcus, your success story is exactly what we want to see. But we do have a fiduciary responsibility to our depositors. Maybe Marcus is right—perhaps the answer isn't stricter lending, but better support after approval. We could partner with business development organizations to provide mentoring and financial management training.

listeningScripts.title: Algorithmic Bias in Hiring Systems
listeningScripts.text: Algorithmic bias in hiring is a serious problem that companies are using as a shortcut without taking responsibility for the consequences. Many organizations now use AI systems to screen resumes, assess candidate fit, and predict job performance. These systems seem objective—they're just mathematics, right? Wrong. These algorithms are trained on historical data, which includes decades of human bias. If women were historically excluded from leadership positions, the algorithm learns that pattern and replicates it. If certain demographics were underrepresented in technical roles, the algorithm reinforces that exclusion. Studies have documented this repeatedly. Amazon famously scrapped their hiring algorithm when they discovered it was discriminating against women. Google's recruiting algorithm showed bias against applicants from historically black colleges. These weren't intentional—that's precisely the problem. The systems' creators didn't set out to discriminate; they just trusted that math was unbiased, when in reality, data is never neutral. My argument is this: companies should not deploy algorithmic hiring systems without rigorous bias testing and external auditing. If you use an algorithm to screen candidates, you're making a business decision, and you're responsible for its outcomes. You can't hide behind the algorithm or claim you didn't know it was biased. Moreover, algorithms eliminate human judgment, nuance, and chance. They can't capture potential, resilience, or growth. Some of the most successful employees wouldn't have passed an algorithm. We need a return to more human-centered hiring while using algorithms cautiously and with oversight.
